10.1109/tcc.2026.3753585: Detecting zero-day attacks in federated streaming networks is challenging because clients observe heterogeneous and evolving traffic, while ground-truth labels for incoming traffic may be delayed, limited, or unavailable for subsequent model updating and evaluation. We propose FedTrident, a communication-efficient open-world federated intrusion detection system that combines personalized per-class reconstruction with federated threshold calibration. Each client maintains private class-specific autoencoders and learns class-aware rejection thresholds from known-class traffic. Federation exchanges only one scalar threshold per known class, rather than raw data, gradients, embeddings, prototypes, or model parameters. During streaming inference, FedTrident identifies the best-matching class using reconstruction error and makes an online known/unknown decision based on the corresponding threshold. Rejected samples can subsequently undergo guarded novelty discovery without altering the immediate decision. We evaluate FedTrident across CICIDS2018, 5G-NIDD, ToN-IoT, and Edge-IIoTset under stationary non-IID, concept-drift, and zero-day evolution scenarios. The results show that per-class reconstruction and federated thresholding provide a useful balance between known-class recognition, false-unknown control, and open-world detection while substantially reducing communication relative to full model exchange.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3753654: The verifiable and lightweight multi-round secure federated learning framework proposed by Li et al. is claimed to achieve dropout resilience, lightweight parameter reuse, and verification of the server's aggregation results. However, this comment identifies plaintext-gradient leakage caused by the combination of long-term private key reconstruction during dropout recovery and cross-round key reuse. Consequently, the aggregation server (AS) can use the reconstructed long-term private key to recover the client's plaintext gradient when the client participates in a later round. Theoretical analysis shows that this plaintext-gradient leakage occurs under both the malicious and the honest-but-curious (HBC) AS threat models.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3753855: As the low-altitude economy expands, Low-Altitude Wireless Networks (LAWN) are critical for UAV-based emergency response, particularly for pixel-level semantic segmentation in complex post-disaster environments. However, multi-UAV collaborative perception faces a fundamental computation-communication trade-off. Heavy local computing induces significant processing latency on resource-constrained UAVs, while offloading raw data to a central server suffers from the limited and stochastic capacity of individual air-to-ground channels. Additionally, heterogeneous data transmission delays inevitably lead to spatiotemporal asynchronous deviations among collaborative nodes. To resolve these conflicts, we propose a Federated Variational Inference (FVI) framework that effectively balances model complexity and communication overhead. Instead of exchanging high-dimensional features and model parameters, UAVs distill statistical intent probability vectors for semantic communication. By reasoning in the federated posterior domain, these vectors support uncertainty-aware semantic fusion at the ground server, enabling lightweight collaborative perception. Extensive experiments on a UAV swarm testbed show that, under the evaluated non-IID and channel settings, FVI-Net achieves up to an 18.97 percentage-point improvement in mIoU over the strongest baseline. Results validate the effectiveness of posterior-domain semantic fusion for communication-efficient and robust UAV swarm perception in constrained LAWN scenarios.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3753678: In distributed data stream processing, buffered asynchronous aggregation collects the first returned updates into a buffer and treats them as a representative sample of the population. Under non-IID data and system heterogeneity, this latency-selected stream can be temporally fresh yet statistically unrepresentative: fast client groups may dominate the buffer while slower groups carrying complementary population directions are systematically absent. We formalize this failure mode asdirection-level representation skewand propose DirBridge, a server-side stream-summary framework that corrects the bias without delaying aggregation or storing per-client entire caches. DirBridge compresses update directions with Count Sketch features, clusters clients into spherical direction groups, and refills only the missing group mass using exponential-moving-average (EMA) group memories. The abstraction is group-based rather than identity-based, reducing auxiliary server storage. We show that group-size-aware refill can eliminate the mixture-weight error under an ideal representative condition, and we further bound the residual convergence error. Experiments on vision, character recognition, and speech workloads under synthetic and natural latency traces show that DirBridge improves stream representativeness when direction skew is large, preserves accuracy when skew is low, and incurs modest overhead. These results position direction-group memory as a practical bias-correction abstraction for latency-selected distributed data streams.
10.1109/tfuzz.2026.3752321: Federated learning ensures data privacy but its effectiveness may be compromised under non-IID heterogeneity, which motivates adaptive server-side aggregation. However OWA, despite its rank-based coordinate-wise flexibility, is difficult to deploy because selecting effective weights is non-trivial and fixed profiles may not match round-to-round changes in client update distributions. This paper proposes an online and lightweight adaptation strategy for OWA weights, parameterized by a single temperature variable that generates a smooth, monotonically decreasing weight vector. At each communication round, the server evaluates a small set of candidate temperatures using a held-out proxy set and selects the one that minimizes proxy loss, with exponential smoothing to stabilize the temperature over time. Experiments conducted on 10 classification benchmark datasets under non-IID partitions show that the proposed adaptive variant achieves statistically significant improvements over all considered reference methods at the global level. Aggregated across datasets, FedOWA Adapt improves mean accuracy by approximately 3.3 percentage points over FedAvg and 1.9 percentage points over fixed-weight FedOWA. In terms of log-loss, the proposed method reduces the mean loss by about 0.12 compared with FedAvg and by about 0.15 compared with fixed-weight FedOWA, indicating improved predictive reliability in addition to higher accuracy. The largest dataset-level gains are particularly visible on selected benchmarks, reaching approximately 13.5 percentage points over FedAvg and up to about 7.8 percentage points over fixed-weight FedOWA. Furthermore, a detailed one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis and an ablation study were performed, confirming the robustness of the proposed configuration and showing that the main source of improvement is the repeated round-wise adaptation of the OWA aggregation profile rather than a single fixed or one-shot selected weighting scheme.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3752488: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) are vulnerable to Global Positioning System (GPS) spoofing attacks that threaten navigation integrity. Existing detection approaches face challenges in privacy, computational efficiency, and class imbalance. We propose three progressive frameworks: 1) a lightweight standalone Logistic Regression (LR) model achieving 95.52% accuracy; 2) Federated Learning with LR (FL+LR), which enables collaborative training across CAVs while keeping raw data local and achieves 97.25% accuracy; 3) a Digital Twin-enhanced framework (DT+FL+LR), which integrates simulated spoofing scenarios and DT-based consistency checking and achieves 97.46% accuracy. Evaluation on AVG-Dataset-1 (62,042 samples) shows that DT+FL+LR achieves 90.00% spoofed-class recall and 100.00% precision. The computational analysis indicates potential edge deployment suitability for standalone LR under the evaluated configuration, while FL variants provide improved data locality with competitive performance. Across the evaluated configurations, the AUC increases from 95.02% to 98.10%, indicating improved discrimination capability and potential deployment feasibility under the considered experimental configuration.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3753332: Multi-access Edge Computing (MEC) and Vehicular-Fogs (VFs) are placed nearer to user equipment (UE), reducing propagation latency compared to traditional cloud-based systems and ensuring a high standard of Quality of Service (QoS). Nevertheless, MEC sites can become congested and overloaded during peak traffic periods, such as concerts or sporting events. To address this, offloading techniques can shift intensive computational tasks from devices with limited resources to those with greater capacity, enhancing task performance and thereby increasing battery longevity. This study investigates the offloading within a two-tier framework of MEC and VF, focusing on the offloading of MEC to VF. Maintaining QoS is challenging due to the instability of fog networks caused by high-speed vehicle movement, which disrupts both vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure communications. To mitigate this, we analyze vehicle mobility using a Gauss-Markov Mobility (GMM) model. Our main goal is to reduce the normalized system cost by optimizing both latency and energy consumption while accounting for vehicle mobility. We approach this challenge as a multi-objective optimization problem and develop a reinforcement learning environment. Additionally, we propose an algorithm based on imitation learning called Hybrid PSO-TD3, an enhancement of the TD3 algorithm, to effectively manage these complexities.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3752611: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data, yet model updates may still leak sensitive information. Multi-key homomorphic encryption (MKHE) can protect updates of clients, but existing works still suffer from complex key management, costly dropout handling, and reliance on an honest-but-curious cloud server. Verifiable MPC-based schemes verify the aggregated client set but incur high communication overhead. TEE-assisted designs enhance efficiency but are bottlenecked by the limited TEE memory and vulnerable to attacks by a malicious cloud server. To address these challenges, we propose TMB-BFV, a TEE-assisted BFV variant incorporating client-specific binding keys, upon which we build AegisFed, a secure FL framework. Specifically, i) to reduce TEE memory usage and computation overhead, we design a lightweight key management mechanism; ii) to resist server–client collusion while making ciphertexts containing different client-specific binding terms homomorphically additive, we optimize the ciphertext structure and introduce an authenticated binding mechanism (ABM); iii) to support arbitrary client dropout without additional handling, we develop a TEE-assisted decryption-share generation mechanism. Finally, we provide formal security analysis and extensive experiments. Compared with the latest TEE-based MKHE scheme, AegisFed resists malicious-server privacy attacks with only minimal additional communication overhead. It also significantly reduces per-client TEE memory consumption and lowers client-side and server-side computation overhead by 20–30% and over 30%, respectively.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3752625: Decentralized Federated Learning (DFL) trains models collaboratively without a central server, but asymmetric and time-varying communication often leads to imbalanced information flow and biased aggregation. Most existing methods address this issue with push-sum normalization, which requires maintaining auxiliary normalization states and can accumulate numerical drift, thereby slowing mixing and degrading convergence under limited connectivity. To address this, we propose Pull-in protocol, a receiver-driven decentralized learning frame work for directed time-varying graphs. Instead of relying on indiscriminate broadcasting, each receiver actively pulls models from a budgeted subset of incoming neighbors and constructs a row-stochastic aggregation vector locally. This receiver-side normalization makes the model aggregation step a stable convex combination by design and avoids push-sum-type normaliza tion variables in directed model mixing. To mitigate the bias caused by directed and asymmetric aggregation, we incorporate a gradient-tracking correction mechanism. In Pull-in-GT, the model aggregation matrix is row-stochastic, while the tracking matrix is constructed to be column-stochastic, enabling average preservation of the tracking variable over directed graphs. We establish convergence guarantees under standard smooth non convex objectives and bounded stochastic noise. The resulting bound explicitly separates optimization progress from consensus induced error terms and yields the rate O(T−1/2) quantifies the mixing speed of the induced row-stochastic matrix. Extensive experiments on vision-centric decentralized learning benchmarks demonstrate that Pull-in consistently improves training stability and achieves stronger performance than representative push-sum based DFL baselines across a wide range of network asymmetries.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3753237: In Satellite-Terrestrial Integrated Networks (STIN), distributed Federated Edge Learning (FEL) has become mainstream methods for data processing and analysis. The traditional FEL algorithm assigns devices for local training and satellites for aggregation to perform intelligent prediction and decision-making. However, it adopts a synchronous aggregation mechanism, where model updating is performed only after all devices complete training. Considering the heterogeneous computational frequency of devices and the advanced onboard processing capabilities of satellites, satellites act as participants in collaborative local training. In this paper, we introduce a Data Offloading-enabled Federated Edge Learning (DO-FEL) framework, where devices offload part of their data to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. The LEO satellites also act as Edge Servers (ESs), while the Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) satellite performs global aggregation. In DO-FEL, the dynamic satellite-device visibility and the limited computational frequency of a single satellite incur additional delay for FEL in STIN. Based on this, we propose a Dynamic Route Scheduling (DRS) strategy to optimize multisatellites' assistance for the collaborative training. Meanwhile, we propose an Adaptive Joint Delay-Energy Optimization (AJDEO) strategy. For different task requirements, the AJDEO strategy adjusts the devices' offloading proportion to balance overall delay and energy consumption. Experimental results show that with the DRS strategy, the DO-FEL framework reduces satelliteside delay and further reduces the overall delay. Besides, the proposed framework with two strategies achieves the trade-off between the overall delay and energy consumption compared with other baselines. This paper provides a new perspective for efficient FEL in STIN through flexible data offloading under actual satellite-device visibility.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3752804: In this paper, we propose PVFUnlearn, a privacypreserving and verifiable data circulation framework for edge assisted federated unlearning in hierarchical federated learning systems. Particularly, local model updates are decomposed into sign and magnitude vectors, where additive homomorphic encryption is applied to the magnitude vectors to achieve efficient secure aggregation with reduced cryptographic overhead. To support efficient federated unlearning, edge-level and serverlevel calibration mechanisms are designed in the way that reconstructs calibrated model updates without requiring the participation of clients under non-unlearning edge servers, thereby avoiding expensive retraining from scratch. In addition, homomorphic commitments are integrated into both aggregation and unlearning processes to guarantee aggregation correctness and unlearning verifiability. Extensive experiments conducted on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that PVFUnlearn achieves forgetting performance close to retraining-based federated unlearning while significantly reducing computational and communication overhead. The results further show that PVFUnlearn effectively maintains model utility and provides strong auditability for secure and trustworthy data circulation in edge-assisted federated unlearning systems.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3752851: Federated learning can achieve collaborative training while protecting user privacy and data security, but differences in the performance of participating devices and the diversity of data distributions pose core challenges: 1) highly heterogeneous data reduce the generalization ability of the model; 2) “straggler” clients with limited capabilities or slow responses can significantly affect the system's training stability. However, existing research still cannot collaboratively address these dual issues within a unified framework, resulting in a trade-off between model generalization and system robustness. To tackle these issues, we propose SplitKD, which enhances the model's generalization to data heterogeneity and stability for straggler clients through parameter splitting and freezing, adaptive knowledge distillation, and differentially weighted aggregation. Specifically, SplitKD finely regulates the knowledge transfer from the global model to the local model through parameter splitting and an adaptive knowledge distillation mechanism, enhancing the generalization ability of the model. For straggler clients, we have designed a parameter-splitting-based differentially weighted aggregation strategy that distinguishes model differences by parameters and simultaneously aggregates their local knowledge, enhancing the robustness and compatibility of the global model. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the convergence of SplitKD, and experimental results show that, compared with 12 existing methods, SplitKD effectively mitigates the impact of stragglers on model performance and enhances model generalization.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3752413: Driven by the advancement of Agentic AI, the deployment of autonomous edge agents in safety-critical systems has introduced stringent requirements for privacy-preserving and adaptive intelligence over dynamic and heterogeneous data streams. While Federated Learning (FL) addresses the privacy constraint through collaborative training without sharing raw data, it struggles with the continuously evolving edge data perceived by autonomous agents. To bridge this gap, Federated Continual Learning (FCL) extends the FL paradigm to enable Agentic AI models to incrementally adapt to new tasks and non-stationary distributions, without compromising data privacy. Despite its potential, FCL faces significant challenges in balancing local personalization and global knowledge consolidation, particularly under heterogeneous and imbalanced class distributions across edge agents. Overcoming this dual challenge is critical to robust, adaptive and trustworthy Agentic AI applications at the network edge. In this work, we propose Meta Representation-based Adaptive Personalized Federated Class Incremental Learning (Meta-APFCIL) to tackle these limitations. Each edge agent first performs adaptive meta-training of a shared representation network using its respective exemplar memory within the FL framework. The resulting global representation is then personalized through fine-tuning on each FCL client's current task data and exemplar memory, guided by class-wise logit adjustment to effectively mitigate the bias introduced by class imbalance between current tasks and stored exemplars. As a result, this approach alleviates catastrophic forgetting, enhancing the model's adaptability and retention of previously learned knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate that Meta-APFCIL outperforms key baseline algorithms, achieving an average task accuracy improvement of 23.79% to 32.62% under varying levels of task similarity among clients' data streams. Additionally, it exhibits the lowest task forgetting ratio and the highest generalization capability among FCL clients, enabling trustworthy and adaptive Agentic AI deployment in edge networks.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3752697: Federated learning (FL) can preserve privacy, but it is limited by the coverage of static edge servers and vulnerable to security risks due to the frequent exchange of model parameters. To address these issues, we establish an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted covert FL framework to protect the transmission of local models from detection by an aerial warden. Acting as a flying server, the UAV aggregates local models from distributed ground devices to improve transmission efficiency. We aim to minimize the energy consumption of terrestrial devices in the presence of a severe security threat to the FL, where the warden adopts the minimum error detection probability. To meet the requirements of energy-sensitive applications, the UAV trajectory, transmission power, local accuracy, model upload time, and local computation capacity are jointly optimized. We decompose the optimization problem into three subproblems, and a low-complexity algorithm is developed. Specifically, for a given UAV trajectory, we derive the closed-form solutions for other variables to reduce the computational complexity. The UAV trajectory is then optimized using successive convex approximation. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed UAV-assisted covert FL scheme in minimizing the energy consumption while guaranteeing the secrecy.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3752445: Federated learning (FL) allows distributed devices to collaboratively train models while preserving data privacy, but heterogeneous computation and communication resources create stragglers, slowing training and limiting scalability. Existing methods, such as client selection, asynchronous FL, and partial training, partially address this but often reduce accuracy or disrupt model consistency. We propose FedEL++, a federated elastic learning framework that addresses both computation and communication heterogeneity. FedEL++ introduces a globally coordinated sliding window, anchored to the slowest client, and optimizes block window selection across all clients under a unified runtime constraint. Within each window, elastic tensor selection accounts for computation and communication costs, while a global-aware tensor importance adjustment mitigates model drift under non-iid data. Experiments on real edge devices and large-scale simulations show that FedEL++ achieves faster convergence, lower training time, and reduced memory and energy usage, while maintaining or improving model accuracy compared to existing FL methods.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3752495: Federated Learning in Internet-of-Things networks confronts a fundamental spatio-temporal trade-off driven by statistical heterogeneity and severe client participation sparsity. Traditional optimization frameworks struggle between two suboptimal extremes: instantaneous aggregation in Drop mode, which suffers from persistent sampling variance due to tiny active client subsets, and historical caching in Stale mode, which incurs cumulative spatial divergence and staleness bias from outdated local updates. In this paper, we proposeFederated Trajectory-Aware Displacement Aggregation (FedTADA), an optimization framework formulated in cumulative displacement space. To stabilize scale normalization without stochastic feedback loops,FedTADAintroduces a zero-order probing phase that establishes an exogenous energy reference anchor. Guided by an unnormalized negative entropy regularizer, we derive a scale-equivariant exponential controller that dynamically balances instantaneous descent against historical consensus. Theoretical analysis proves thatFedTADAachieves higher-order variance suppression, accelerating the client-sampling variance decay rate from the standard$\mathcal {O}(1/T)$down to$\mathcal {O}(1/T^{2})$via a joint Lyapunov potential function that strictly neutralizes staleness bias while isolating the irreducible Local-SGD drift floor. Extensive experiments across four distinct modalities under fully trainable end-to-end convolutional architectures demonstrate thatFedTADAachieves significant accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under extreme label skew with zero additional client-side computational or communication overhead.
10.1109/tai.2026.3752417: The client selection of federated learning presents a pivotal dilemma necessitating the harmonization of performance and efficiency. Prevailing studies frame this dilemma within the context of a multi-armed bandit optimization problem. With an expanding client base, the complexity of the task increases exponentially, demanding advanced algorithms to efficiently navigate the decision space. Fuzzy sets offer a clear depiction of the uncertainties associated with client selection, eliminating the need for intricate numerical computations. To this end, this paper proposes a fuzzy client selection (FuzzyCS) method. Specifically, we construct a fuzzy multi-criteria information matrix based on several selection criteria and use it to introduce a criteria-oriented fuzzy selection model. By leveraging the fuzzy rough approximations, we can estimate the fuzzy relationship between the criteria-oriented fuzzy concepts of each client and its likelihood of being selected. FuzzyCS can actively balance performance and efficiency by constructing an adaptive fuzzy approximation set, which incorporates the upper and lower approximate fuzzy rough sets. Experimental results demonstrate that FuzzyCS achieves the top Friedman rank in both performance and efficiency. The code is available athttps://github.com/dqlme/FuzzyCS.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3752635: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks; however, training them from scratch requires substantial computational resources. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as an efficient fine-tuning technique that enables the adaptation of pre-trained LLMs to specific tasks with significantly reduced computational cost. In Federated Learning (FL), mobile clients operate under constrained communication and computational resources, making LoRA particularly important for efficient model adaptation. However, directly applying LoRA in FL can still incur substantial communication overhead, particularly in wireless environments. To address this, we propose a novel framework, called Federated LoRA with Structural Sparsification (FLR-SS), which reduces communication cost by sparsifying LoRA matrices through the removal of rows and columns with the smallest norms, thereby preserving the most informative components. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis of FLR SS and formulate the selection of rows and columns as a bi convex optimization problem, which can be solved efficiently. Extensive experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate that FLR-SS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving accuracy improvements of 1.66% to 8.63% while reducing communication traffic by 21.42% to 53.33%.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3752869: Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR) effectively alleviates the data sparsity problem by transferring knowledge from source domains to target domains. To address growing data privacy concerns, Federated Learning (FL) has been incorporated into CDR, enabling multiple clients to collaborate without exposing raw data. However, most existing federated CDR methods still rely on overlapping entities to bridge different clients. Under strict privacy constraints, such correspondences are often unavailable, causing structural misalignment across isolated clients and weakening cross-domain knowledge transfer. To address this problem, we propose DFTCDR, aDecomposedFederatedTransfer framework forCross-DomainRecommendation. DFTCDR performs cluster-level structural alignment across disjoint domains through complementary modeling of transferable cluster-level structures and local residual interaction patterns. Specifically, we employ PARAFAC2-based tensor decomposition to learn transferable cluster-level structural prototypes, which act as virtual anchors for mapping isolated clients into a shared structural space. To balance transferability and personalization, DFTCDR further models local residual information through intra-domain graph propagation. In addition, a consistency-aware knowledge filtering mechanism evaluates whether each global prototype is consistent with the client local interaction semantics and retains only locally consistent prototypes to mitigate negative transfer. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that DFTCDR outperforms baselines without relying on overlapping entities. Additional experiments demonstrate its overall effectiveness and domain sparsity robustness.
10.1109/tpds.2026.3752125: Next-generation Internet of Things (IoT) applications increasingly span across autonomous administrative entities, necessitating silo-cooperative scheduling to leverage diverse computational resources while preserving data privacy. However, realizing efficient cooperation faces significant challenges arising from infrastructure heterogeneity, Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) workload shifts, and the inherent risks of adversarial environments. Existing approaches, relying predominantly on centralized coordination or independent learning, fail to address the incompatibility of state-action spaces across heterogeneous silos and lack robustness against malicious attacks. To address these challenges, this paper proposes DeFRiS, a Decentralized Federated Reinforcement Learning framework for robust and scalable Silo-cooperative IoT application scheduling. DeFRiS integrates three synergistic innovations: (i) an action-space-agnostic policy utilizing candidate resource scoring to enable seamless knowledge transfer across heterogeneous silos; (ii) a silo-optimized local learning mechanism combining Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) with clipped policy updates to resolve sparse delayed reward challenges; and (iii) a Dual-Track Non-IID robust decentralized aggregation protocol leveraging gradient fingerprints for similarity-aware knowledge transfer and anomaly detection, and gradient tracking for optimization momentum. Extensive experiments on a distributed testbed with 20 heterogeneous silos and realistic IoT workloads demonstrate that DeFRiS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, DeFRiS reduces average response time by 6.4% and energy consumption by 7.2% compared to the best-performing baseline, while lowering tail latency risk (CVaR$_{0.95}$) by 10.4% and achieving near-zero deadline violations. Furthermore, extensive experiments reveal that DeFRiS achieves over 3 times better performance retention as the system scales and over 8 times better stability in adversarial environments compared to the best-performing baseline.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3751990: The space-air-ground integrated network (SAGIN) is expected to support ubiquitous edge intelligence in sixth-generation (6G) mobile networks, where federated learning (FL) can exploit distributed data without exposing raw samples. In SAGIN, resource-constrained ground devices and heterogeneous wireless links make synchronous FL vulnerable to stragglers, which may cause excessive training delay. A naive attempt to reduce this delay by excluding straggling devices can introduce distribution drift under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, especially when these devices contain rare or complementary samples. To address these coupled latency and robustness issues, this paper proposes a hierarchical split federated learning (HSFL) framework for SAGIN. In this framework, ground devices execute shallow model layers, Autonomous Aerial Vehicles (AAVs) process the remaining layers and perform edge aggregation, and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites conduct satellite-level aggregation. We derive a convergence upper bound to capture the effects of split layer selection, user association, and data distribution on convergence. A joint optimization problem is formulated to minimize training delay by optimizing split layer selection, device-AAV association, AAV-LEO association, and communication and computing resource allocation. To solve this mixed-integer nonlinear problem, we first design a tabu-assisted block coordinate descent (TA-BCD) algorithm that alternately updates topology association, resource allocation, and split layer selection. We further develop a robust device-admission extension of TA-BCD (RDA-TA-BCD), which jointly optimizes device admission, topology association, and resource scheduling and incorporates federated unlearning to approximately remove the historical model influence of excluded devices. The resulting scheduler protects data-critical bottleneck devices while removing redundant ones, thereby balancing delay reduction with model robustness. Simulation results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that the proposed algorithms reduce training delay while maintaining model accuracy under heterogeneous SAGIN and non-IID data settings.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3751908: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a compelling paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning, allowing multiple clients to collaboratively train a global model by transmitting locally computed gradients to a central server without exposing their private data. Nonetheless, recent studies find that the gradients exchanged in the FL system are also vulnerable to privacy leakage, e.g., an attacker can invert shared gradients to reconstruct sensitive data by leveraging pre-trained generative adversarial networks (GAN) as prior knowledge. However, existing attacks simply perform gradient inversion in the latent space of the GAN model, which limits their expression ability and generalizability. To tackle these challenges, we propose Gradient Inversion over Feature Domains (GIFD), which disassembles the GAN model and searches the hierarchical features of the intermediate layers. Instead of optimizing only over the initial latent code, we progressively change the optimized layer, from the initial latent space to intermediate layers closer to the output images. In addition, we design a regularizer to avoid unreal image generation by adding a small ${l_{1}}$ ball constraint to the searching range. We also extend GIFD to the out-of-distribution (OOD) setting, which weakens the assumption that the training sets of GANs and FL tasks obey the same data distribution. Furthermore, we consider the challenging OOD scenario of label inconsistency and propose a label mapping technique as an effective solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can achieve high-quality reconstruction and outperform competitive baselines across a variety of FL scenarios.
10.1109/tits.2026.3740049: Transportation digital twins (DTs) can support proactive traffic management and operations by maintaining dynamic virtual representations of transportation systems. Developing transportation DTs requires accurate lane-level geometry, which is commonly obtained from static maps or dedicated sensors. However, these sources limit scalability and may fail to reflect changes in roadway configuration in a timely manner. Moreover, transportation DTs rely on large volumes of multi-source data, and centralizing these data across locations raises privacy and communication concerns. To address these limitations, we introduce Geo-ORBIT (Geometrical Operational Roadway Blueprint with Integrated Twin), a decentralized, privacy-aware framework that adapts to geometry changes. Geo-ORBIT combines label-free lane detection from roadside cameras, DT synchronization, and federated meta-learning. Its core model, GeoLane, infers lane geometry from vehicle trajectories without human labels. Meta-GeoLane adapts the detection parameters to each scene, while FedMeta-GeoLane learns a shared adaptation across sites under federated updates that keep raw data local. Geo-ORBIT connects to SUMO and CARLA to render highway scenes and replay traffic, and supports a closed-loop update in which detected changes in lane geometry are propagated to the running simulation. Validated against independent human annotations on real-world data, the detected geometry achieves an error of approximately 3 m, representing nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement over the public map that supervises training. Moreover, FedMeta-GeoLane transfers a single global model across sites without per-site training and reduces per-camera communication by more than 99% relative to centralizing trajectories. The framework is publicly available athttps://github.com/raynbowy23/FedMeta-GeoLane.git
10.1109/tnse.2026.3750978: Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) anomaly detection faces significant challenges due to dynamic network topologies, non-IID data distributions, high-dimensional multi-modal features, and privacy preservation. Conventional federated learning (FL) approaches suffer from high communication overhead, poor adaptation to concept drift, and difficulty in preserving cross-modal correlations. To address these limitations, we propose a dynamic federated learning (DFL) framework that integrates attention-based generative anomaly detection with tensorized aggregation. Client-side multi-modal statistics, including detection losses, KL divergence, attention distributions, PCA features, and metadata, are unified into a six-mode tensor on the server, which is incrementally updated via incremental tensor-train decomposition (ITTD). This enables efficient updates, preserves structural correlations across modalities, and provides explicit monitoring of drift through rank variation and reconstruction error. A hard-soft coupled decision mechanism further selects and weights client updates by combining adaptive thresholding, latent-space clustering, and variance-aware weighting. Experimental results demonstrate that on the IoT-23 dataset, our method achieves an F1 score of 95.89% with a reduced false positive rate (FPR) of 1.58%, while on the SECOM manufacturing dataset it attains 95.02% F1 with 2.04% FPR under the full tensorized DFL setting. Moreover, the proposed DFL with tensor aggregation reduces communication overhead compared with baseline FL methods, indicating its potential to enable scalable, privacy-preserving anomaly detection in dynamic IIoT environments.
10.1109/tifs.2026.3751573: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) has garnered increasing interest thanks to its ability to harness the representational power of graphs, while its development is still impeded by privacy issues stemming from the direct upload of a participant’s local model. In this study, we address privacy concerns of FGL by Differential Privacy (DP), and devise a novel graph-level framework for Heterogeneous Federated Graph Learning with Differential Privacy (DP-HFGL). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to investigate graph-level classification tasks in federated setting, while providing rigorous DP guarantee. The primary challenges in this work stem from the intra-client feature and structure heterogeneity among graphs, inter-client statistical heterogeneity in local distribution shifts and DP-required noise injection. Specifically, these factors bring significant variance to the model gradients, leading to unstable training and utility degradation. To address these issues, DP-HFGL applies a dual-channel model to process feature and structure information separately and shares only structural information with the server, which significantly mitigates the impact of heterogeneity under noise perturbation. To further enhance the overall performance, we perform DP operations only on the shared structure knowledge to naturally reduce the norm of local updates before clipping, making local updates adaptive to the DP operations. Extensive experiments on several types of datasets, including Molecules, Proteins, Social Networks and Computer Vision, demonstrate the effectiveness of DP-HFGL in federated graph learning.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3751775: This paper presents an invariant federated learning framework for resource-constrained edge intelligence. The framework first identifies and excludes low-value or aberrant clients, and then enforces model-level invariance to preserve generalization. Motivated by pretraining-based client valuation, we show that some clients may have negligible or even detrimental contributions to global aggregation under severe heterogeneity or asynchrony. Accordingly, we propose a practical exit strategy based on client utility and delay, which removes such clients from the main training loop to protect in-distribution (ID) performance. To maintain robust performance for excluded and resource-constrained clients, we introduce FedIPG (Federated Learning with Invariant Penalty for Generalization), which promotes approximate orthogonality between invariant and heterogeneous parameter components through a gradient-based penalty. We provide theoretical analysis showing that low-value client exit can improve aggregation and that FedIPG tightens an upper bound on out-of-distribution (OOD) risk without increasing communication overhead during formal training. Extensive experiments on four domain-generalization benchmarks and multiple client scales demonstrate that the combined exit + FedIPG framework improves ID accuracy, enhances OOD generalization over recent baselines, and maintains stable convergence. Visualization results further indicate that FedIPG reduces reliance on confounding features and encourages more task-relevant feature usage.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3751266: The growing scale of deep models is straining learning at the edge: resource-constrained devices struggle to train locally, and heterogeneous wireless links create communication bottlenecks, resulting in stragglers. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose a multi-edge split federated learning (MESFL) framework, which facilitates split federated learning (SFL) over a mobile edge computing (MEC) system. The MEC system comprises client devices, edge servers, and a federated (fed) server. Server-side sub-model aggregation is performed on each edge server. The periodic federated aggregation is performed on the fed server. We consider a practical resource-limited scenario where all client devices and edge servers have limited computation and memory capacities. The proposed MESFL framework jointly optimizes sub-model offloading decisions, layer splitting, and federated aggregation frequency to improve the learning efficiency. We formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize the learning convergence bound subject to latency and memory constraints. The problem is NP-hard, and we apply an exact finite-interval decomposition with interval-level pruning, which yields a globally optimal solution when the fixed-interval subproblems are solved to optimality, or a certified anytime solution under a time limit. Extensive experiments on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets with ResNet-18, together with an architecture study on CIFAR-10 using VGG-11 and MobileNetV2, validate the effectiveness of the proposed MESFL framework. We compare MESFL with seven baseline methods in terms of test accuracy and training latency. We further conduct an ablation analysis to study the effects of offloading and layer splitting decisions.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3750980: Personalized federated learning (PFL) addresses statistical heterogeneity by adapting models to individual clients, but its utility can degrade substantially under client-level differential privacy (DP). Two major causes are rigid parameter partitioning and isotropic update clipping, which overlook the continuous importance distribution and distinct optimization roles of model parameters. We propose FedVPC, a privacy-preserving PFL framework consisting of two complementary components. First, the Variable Hierarchical Pyramid (VHP) uses an empirical diagonal Fisher proxy to softly stratify parameters into personalized, bridging, and globally aligned groups. Second, the Parameter-Customized Constraint (PCC) applies group-aware regularization before client-level clipping and Gaussian perturbation to reduce optimization distortion. We establish a client-level DP guarantee through update clipping, distributed Gaussian perturbation, and RDP accounting, while secure aggregation restricts the server to aggregate-only observation. We also characterize convergence under heterogeneous data. Experiments on five datasets show that FedVPC consistently outperforms representative DP-FL and DP-PFL baselines, with improvements of up to 7.66 percentage points across the evaluated settings. FedVPC also demonstrates robustness to data heterogeneity, client scale, and model architecture while showing empirical resistance to gradient inversion under the evaluated diagnostic setting.
10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3750827: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without exposing raw data, thus ensuring privacy compliance. However, data heterogeneity among participants introduces significant challenges for effective federated optimization. While prior research has attempted to address this issue typically by regularizing local updates or fine-tuning the global model, the aggregation weights in most FL frameworks are still determined solely by dataset size. This simplistic strategy may hinder convergence and limit overall model effectiveness, highlighting the ongoing need for adaptive and secure aggregation methods. This paper proposes FedAED, a novel FL framework that Adaptively adjusts aggregation weights through Editing Directions derived from client model updates. The editing direction vector encodes the semantic trajectory of local model updates, effectively capturing the underlying data heterogeneity across clients. This approach enables more accurate aggregation that is well aligned with global optimization goals, preserves privacy, and requires no auxiliary data. As a result, FedAED enhances both the stability and generalization ability of the global model. Comprehensive experimental results confirm that our approach consistently surpasses strong baselines and significantly improves the effectiveness of FL under heterogeneous environments.
10.1109/tifs.2026.3750716: This paper studies a novel quantum federated learning (QFL) framework that leverages inherent quantum noise to enforce differential privacy (DP) and protect model updates from information leakage in current near-term quantum devices. Specifically, we achieve targeted DP guarantees during model training by (i) varying the number of measurement shots, and (ii) leveraging unavoidable depolarizing channel noise. To adapt privacy levels based on varying training conditions, we further introduce an adaptive DP strategy using a multi-armed bandit (MAB) agent at each quantum device, enabling dynamic control over the trade-off between privacy and model performance. Moreover, we present a rigorous convergence analysis of our proposed QFL-DP model. Our theoretical analysis and numerical evaluation reveal the following key properties: i) the global QFL-DP model converges to a bounded error floor, which indicates that, despite leveraging inherent quantum noise for DP, the model’s performance remains stable, making our approach suitable for real-world QFL applications; ii) a clear trade-off exists between privacy guarantees and model accuracy, and the adaptive MAB strategy further enhances this trade-off by enabling adaptive privacy budgeting with efficient noise allocation based on training dynamics and client needs; iii) our theoretical results are consistent with simulations, thereby demonstrating the superiority of the proposed framework over baseline approaches in terms of training accuracy, adaptive privacy preservation, and robustness against adversarial examples. Overall, the results highlight a tunable trade-off between privacy and robustness, offering an efficient and secure QFL solution for current nearterm quantum devices.
10.1109/tifs.2026.3750691: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without directly sharing data, thereby offering effective privacy guarantees. However, the decentralized architecture of FL makes it vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries can compromise a subset of clients to inject malicious updates, causing the global model to misbehave on specific trigger inputs. The existing defenses typically rely on static rules or auxiliary validation data, which often lack adaptability against evolving attack strategies or introduce privacy risks and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose GameRLFed, a robust defense framework that formulates the FL security problem as a repeated game with incomplete information. Without requiring any auxiliary data, the server infers the malicious tendencies of each client based on current updates and historical observations and employs reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the aggregation weights for mitigating backdoor effects. Moreover, attackers adaptively evolve their strategies in response to the behavior of the server to maximize the effectiveness of their attacks while minimizing the risk of detection, resulting in complex game interactions. Theoretically, we prove that GameRLFed can converge to a near-optimal global model under adversarial dynamics. Extensive experiments conducted across multiple datasets and attack types show that GameRLFed outperforms six baseline methods in terms of robustness, adaptability, and computational efficiency.
10.1109/tmlcn.2026.3750808: The paradigm shift towards Softwarized Edge Computing (SEC) and 6G networks necessitates the deployment of deep learning models as flexible, lightweight Virtual Network Functions (VNFs). However, training high-performance Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in such resource-constrained, heterogeneous environments presents significant challenges. Existing low-rank adaptation methods often rely on static rank allocations or require heavy pre-trained backbones, limiting their applicability for training from scratch or adapting to novel edge domains. In this paper, we propose GILoRaT++, a unified framework for resource-efficient training and fine-tuning. We introduce a novelRank Demand Score, grounded in gradient sensitivity analysis, to replace global greedy heuristics. This metric allows the network to autonomously identify layer-wise capacity bottlenecks, incrementing the rank of specific layers only when their sensitivity to the loss function dictates necessity. Furthermore, we propose GILoRaFT, a Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategy that combines aggressive SVD-based compression with feature distillation and weight perturbation control to adapt models with minimal parameter overhead. Finally, we address the challenge of Federated Learning (FL) in heterogeneous edge environments with a case study. We propose a budget-constrained rank allocation scheme and solve the low-rank rotational ambiguity problem using Orthogonal Procrustes Alignment. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Brain Tumor MRI datasets demonstrate that GILoRAT++ achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with up to 20× parameter reduction compared to full-rank baselines, while offering superior convergence speed in federated settings.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3741038: Statistical heterogeneity in 6 G Internet of Vehicles (IoV) networks severely limits standard federated learning paradigms, leading to significant weight divergence and suboptimal personalization. We proposed ACPFL-KD, an adaptive clustering personalized federated learning framework that synthesizes dynamic topology reconstruction with data-free, duallayer knowledge distillation. Diverging from static clustering regimes and conventional federated distillation, our Affinity Propagation strategy leverages lightweight feature representations and a theoretically grounded, regularized similarity metric to autonomously restructure the network topology without predefined cluster constraints, even with sparse client participation. We devise a synergistic dual-layer knowledge-sharing architecture to stabilize convergence. At the intra-cluster level, coordinatewise median aggregation yields robust teacher models that guide clients in extracting group consensus; simultaneously, an inter-cluster adaptive regularization strategy fuses heterogeneous knowledge increments to effectively bridge information silos. Experiments on five datasets, including the real-world autonomous driving dataset BDD100 K, together with rigorous theoretical convergence analysis, validate this framework. In highly non- IID settings, ACPFL-KD consistently outperforms state-of-theart personalization and distillation baselines (e.g., Fed-DFA, FedPer), achieving superior classification accuracy, particularly in complex mobility scenarios. Furthermore, it maintains this lead while demonstrating accelerated convergence and drastically reducing central communication bandwidth overhead compared to current baselines. Future work will explore cross-domain adaptation to further enhance scalability in dynamic, real-world deployments.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3750240: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving traffic perception in roadside unit (RSU)-assisted cellular vehicle-to-everything (C-V2X) networks, but vehicle deletion requires removing both historical model influence and subsequent communication participation. In cell-free C-V2X, deletion further affects aggregation, RSU association, vehicle-to-RSU (V2R) transmission, and energy accounting. We propose traffic context-directed Fisher corrective unlearning (TC-FCU), which uses a diagonal empirical-Fisher preconditioner and momentum-stabilized updates for low-cost corrective retraining with traffic-context-adaptive correction. We further formulate machine unlearning (MU) execution as deletion scheduling under deadline and processing-capacity constraints, jointly considering pre-deletion resource consumption, corrective unlearning cost, and the marginal network-side energy change of the remaining vehicles. We analyze the Fisher–Hessian relation under explicit assumptions, local descent, and deletion-cost monotonicity. Simulations show that TC-FCU approaches full-retraining forgetting quality with much lower runtime, while Proposed Timing reduces normalized cost over benchmark scheduling schemes.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3749663: Federated edge learning (FEL) has significant advantages in terms of protecting user privacy and reducing communication overhead in vehicular networks. Improving learning accuracy and minimizing communication overhead by adjusting resource allocation strategies is the research focus of FEL. Although FEL helps enhance privacy through data encryption, information leakage caused by localization errors remains a challenging problem. To address this issue, we utilize the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) to calculate the vehicle localization errors, filter out vehicles that meet the localization accuracy requirements, and then select vehicles from them to participate in FEL. Furthermore, a joint optimization problem for dynamic resource allocation is proposed, in order to balance the learning accuracy and communication overhead. The optimization problem is formulated as a Markov decision process (MDP). To solve such MDP, we adopt a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based approach and propose a novel CRLB-based FEL algorithm, i.e., FC-TD3,which structurally integrates a reliability-filtering mechanism into the twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) framework. By employing this mechanism, the algorithm dynamically constructs a high-confidence candidate pool to select vehicles that meet localization accuracy requirements, thereby ensuring that only reliable agents participate in the FEL process. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional algorithms in dealing with such problems. Finally, we conduct simulations to validate the performance of the algorithm and clarify the impact of different parameters on system performance through numerical analysis.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3748952: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across distributed clients without centralizing their data. Its open participation exposes aggregation to model-poisoning and Byzantine attacks, so the server must admit only updates that advance the shared objective. Existing defenses rely on protocol level authentication or statistical robustness. Neither evaluates whether an admitted update moves the global model along the task-induced descent direction. Under non-IID data and partial participation, authenticated and statistically plausible updates can jointly push training off task. We introduce SATF (Selective Admission via Task-directional Filtering), a server-side admission mechanism. SATF ranks updates by their directional alignment with a round-wise reference direction and applies an interquartile-range gate on update magnitudes. It needs no trusted dataset and does not use the Byzantine fraction as an algorithmic input. We bound the adversarial perturbation of the reference direction and give a worst-case benign-majority bound for the retained set, extended to the accepted set under a stated gate condition. We derive a one-step descent bound and a sublinear multi-round convergence rate up to an explicit Byzantine-dependent bias term, and we characterize the scaling detection threshold of the magnitude gate. On Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with one hundred clients and three random seeds, against FedAvg, Trimmed Mean, FLAME-Clip, FLTrust, and Multi-Krum, SATF, at moderate heterogeneity, attains the highest mean accuracy under strong-replacement attacks on CIFAR-10 and stays within two points of the best method under strong replacement on Fashion-MNIST and under mixed attacks on both datasets. We also report its limitations under high heterogeneity and scaling attacks.
10.1109/tce.2026.3749446: The rapid growth of consumer electronics (CE) systems introduces significant challenges for Federated Learning (FL), particularly in managing device heterogeneity, ensuring data privacy, and achieving personalized model adaptation. However, existing FL methods often struggle to adequately capture complex multi-level relationships or effectively balance global knowledge sharing with nuanced local adaptation, particularly with heterogeneous consumer devices and user-specific service contexts. In this paper, we propose a Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) framework with Large Language Model (LLM)-Guided Graph Representation, named PFL-LLMGR, to model intricate cross-device semantic relationships, facilitate multilevel collaboration, and achieve refined personalization without sharing raw data in an end-edge-cloud architecture. Specifically, an LLM is incorporated to analyze lightweight device metadata on the cloud, so as to guide global graph pruning and node fusion while capturing deeper semantic relationships. A local subgraph construction scheme based on multi-source information fusion is then introduced on the edge, and an edge-deployed Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) is trained to fuse features within these subgraphs, generating enhanced representations distributed back to clients. Furthermore, local models are decomposed into feature extractors that participate in edge aggregation and personalized classifiers that remain on clients. An alternating training scheme is developed to synchronize local model training based on edge-fused features while GCN parameters are fixed, and update the edge GCN using client-side feedback while local parameters are fixed, effectively balancing shared knowledge and local adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, DIGIT, and the CE-oriented Office-Home benchmark demonstrate that PFL-LLMGR achieves consistently competitive and often superior accuracy under label heterogeneity, domain shift, and varying client scales, with an improvement of up to 2.65 percentage points over the strongest baseline on Office-Home withK= 50, offering valuable insights for advanced FL in consumer electronics systems, especially in enhancing collaborative intelligence and personalization.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3749791: Federated Learning (FL) allows collaborative training with local gradients uploaded by clients instead of sharing their raw data. For scenarios like the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) where large volumes of sensitive driving data are generated, cryptography techniques are leveraged to encrypt or mask the local gradients. However, these privacy-preserving approaches are vulnerable to poisoning attacks, as it is difficult to detect malicious gradients within the ciphertext. Potential poisoning attacks in IoVs can significantly impact the accuracy and performance of the system. To combat this issue, we propose PAFL, a privacy-awareness and adversarial-resilient FL model. At the heart of our method is an aggregation mechanism delicately designed to protect private data while being robust against poisoning attacks. During the aggregation process, self mask and gradient mask are devised on the original gradient to prevent privacy leakage. Furthermore, an evaluation mechanism is implemented to identify and filter out malicious vehicles from subsequent model updates, ultimately defending against poisoning attacks. Our model suits the characteristics of IoVs, reducing the communication overhead from$O(n^{2})$to approximately$O(nlogn)$, while effectively mitigating poisoning attacks and safeguarding privacy. Experiments have validated the effectiveness and feasibility of PAFL in large-scale IoVs, which outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by reducing the aggregation time by nearly 8 times.
10.1109/tase.2026.3749430: While numerous machine learning approaches have been proposed for machine remaining useful life (RUL) prediction, they typically rely on centralized datasets for model training. In real-world scenarios, however, obtaining these datasets is often impractical, since machine monitoring data (e.g., from aircraft engines) is proprietary to various stakeholders (e.g., airline companies) and cannot be freely shared. Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling collaborative training of a global model without requiring direct data sharing. However, federated RUL prediction models often face performance degradation due to the decentralized and non-uniform distribution of training data. Recently, large language models (LLMs) pretrained on web-scale datasets have demonstrated strong generalization capability in representation learning, suggesting their potential to provide shared representations for mitigating data heterogeneity in federated RUL prediction. Specifically, frozen prompt embeddings provide a shared external target representation over RUL labels. This fixed representation serves as a partially ordinal regularizer that encourages compatible feature learning across clients with heterogeneous local data. In this paper, we propose FedLER, a novel framework that enhances federated RUL prediction model training by incorporating frozen LLM-derived prompt embeddings through knowledge distillation. To address the mismatch between the generic embedding space and the specific domains of clients’ local datasets, we further design an alignment module that adapts the embeddings before distillation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedLER significantly improves the performance of federated RUL prediction models under various FL scenarios.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3748545: Model heterogeneity poses a significant challenge in Heterogeneous Federated Learning (HtFL). In scenarios with diverse model architectures, directly aggregating model parameters is impractical, leading HtFL methods to incorporate an extra guiding objective alongside the original local objective on each client to facilitate collaboration. However, this often results in a mismatch between the guiding and local objectives. To resolve this mismatch and ensure the guiding objective consistently benefits each client's original objective rather than interfering with it, we propose Federated Learning-to-Guide (FedL2G), a federated method that adaptively learns to guide local training in a meta-learning manner. In this way, the client can learn the necessary knowledge from the process of aligning globally shared information, thereby compensating for the required information for its local task. We theoretically prove that FedL2G achieves a non-convex convergence rate of $\mathcal {O}(1/T)$. We also conduct extensive experiments across three types of data heterogeneity and six model heterogeneity settings, using 14 heterogeneous model architectures (e.g., CNNs and ViTs). The results show that FedL2G consistently outperforms 12 state-of-the-art methods in terms of test accuracy (both in-distribution and out-of-distribution) as well as communication and computational overhead, across standard benchmark datasets and specialized medical scenarios.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3748922: Existing AI-based intrusion detection systems are typically trained for specific network environments, leading to significant performance degradation when deployed in different settings or exposed to evolving attack strategies. We propose GRIDS (Generalized Representation-based Intrusion Detection System), a federated contrastive learning framework for cross-environment intrusion detection that keeps raw traffic data local. GRIDS employs a Transformer-based encoder trained with supervised contrastive learning across distributed network environments, learning a shared representation without exchanging sensitive traffic data. The encoder embeds network flow features into a latent space where semantically similar traffic patterns cluster together, enabling effective anomaly detection via k-nearest neighbor scoring. Evaluated on four heterogeneous NetFlow datasets, GRIDS outperforms existing federated IDS baselines on average with a single unified model. In leave-one-out cross-validation, a substantial portion of the detection capability of GRIDS transfers to network environments unseen during training, and the level of transfer varies across target networks. Deployment at such a network requires no labeled attack data or fine-tuning. It uses the benign traffic of the network as the kNN reference set and its unlabeled traffic for normalization and threshold calibration. The framework targets deployments in which a single model protects multiple heterogeneous networks.
10.1109/tgcn.2026.3748550: Existing particle-based Bayesian federated learning algorithms face challenges in substantial maintenance expenses in terms of computation, storage, and communication of particles, as well as the oversight of inherent correlation among particles in the lower layers of network parameters. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose a federated low-rank Bayesian approximation learning algorithm via Stein variational gradient descent (FedLoBA) in this paper. Specifically, we verify the occurrence of low-rank subspace among parameters in the same layer of particles through experiment and then design a low-rank Bayesian approximation module to decrease the maintenance costs and improve the shareability among particles. The lower and upper bounds of the discrepancy between the original and approximate posterior distributions are established theoretically. Furthermore, an aggregation refinement strategy has been developed to eliminate extra cross terms during the particle aggregation stage. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed FedLoBA algorithm exhibits superior prediction accuracy compared to other benchmark algorithms, as well as significant efficiency advantages in terms of computation, storage, and communication over its full-dimensional competitor.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3747879: This paper investigates age-of-information (AoI) aware federated learning over wireless networks with finite speed pinching antennas. In contrast to existing studies that assume an infinitely high antenna moving speed, a practical round based training procedure is considered, where the pinching antenna is repositioned during the local training phase and its feasible movement range depends on the selected devices. This creates a new coupling among device selection, antenna placement, local training time, model uploading time, and AoI evolution. To characterize the impact of antenna moving speed, the rate gain over the fixed antenna and the gap to the infinite speed benchmark are analyzed. Subsequently, an overall AoI minimization problem is formulated under a round latency deadline by jointly optimizing the selected device set and the pinching antenna position. A coalitional game based device selection algorithm is proposed, where finite speed antenna placement is incorporated into the coalition utility evaluation. For antenna placement, the optimal search region is derived by exploiting the mobility constraint and device location span, based on which a branch-and-bound (BnB) algorithm is developed to obtain the global optimum. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme can accelerate learning convergence, reduce the sum AoI, and improve device participation compared with baseline schemes, demonstrating the potential of pinching antennas for enhancing federated learning through flexible spatial reconfiguration.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3748054: Federated continual learning (FCL) has attracted considerable interest by enabling local clients to continually acquire knowledge from new tasks. However, most FCL methods assume that the global server has prior knowledge of the arrival times and number of categories for new tasks, which is unrealistic in the real world. Furthermore, they neglect the importance of positive inter-task semantic relationships when learning new tasks and are significantly affected by irrelevant relationships from old tasks, thereby exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novelTaskRelevance-drivenPromptExpansion (TRPE) model. Specifically, to eliminate the reliance on prior knowledge of new tasks, we propose an out-of-distribution detector to identify the arrival of new tasks within local clients, along with a radius-adaptive DBSCAN to infer the quantity of categories in new tasks on the proxy server. Moreover, to explore positive inter-task relationships, we calculate the affinity between the original gradient for learning new task and its gradient orthogonal to the feature space of old tasks to evaluate semantic relevance between old and new tasks from a global perspective. Then, we use this global task relevance to determine the key-prompt pair for new tasks and identify highly related old tasks. After concatenating their prompts for training, we can leverage such positive inter-task relations to improve the continual learning of newly arriving tasks. To balance the learning of new tasks and the forgetting of old ones, a soft orthogonality constraint is applied to the local key and prompt gradients. Experiments spanning diverse datasets and backbones confirm the efficacy of our TRPE model.
10.1109/tce.2026.3747875: We present FedGuard-XAI, a novel federated learning (FL) framework for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) environments, combining Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture with SHAP-based explainability and gradient-based adversarial defense mechanisms for breast cancer detection. Our approach addresses the critical challenges of data privacy, model robustness, and clinical interpretability in cross-continental healthcare settings where sensitive medical imaging data must remain decentralized across distributed IoMT devices and institutional networks. We evaluated FedGuard-XAI using a private dataset of 8,220 mammograms from South Asian populations (collected from five tertiary hospitals in India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh) combined with public datasets including TCGA-BRCA (1,098 patients), CBIS-DDSM (2,620 cases), and INbreast (410 images). The FL framework incorporates a novel Differential Privacy-Preserving Attention Mechanism (DP-PAM) achieving 94.3% accuracy while maintaining ε = 2.1 privacy guarantee. Building on this privacy foundation, adversarial robustness was evaluated against FGSM, PGD, and C&W attacks, retaining 86.4% average accuracy across all attack settings (a 7.9 percentage-point degradation), compared with 51.5–71.0 points for baseline models. The framework’s explainability module identified candidate biomarkers in South Asian populations, suggesting distinct tissue density patterns that warrant further clinical validation, while enabling secure collaborative learning across geographically distributed IoMT healthcare systems without centralizing sensitive patient data. Clinical validation with radiologists across three experience levels demonstrated 7.4% diagnostic accuracy improvement and 31% reduction in evaluation time, establishing FedGuard-XAI as a practical solution for privacy-preserving, robust, and interpretable AI deployment in real-world IoMT-enabled healthcare environments.
10.1109/tnse.2026.3748286: The rapid development of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the open and broadcast nature of wireless links such as 5G/6G have made user privacy a critical issue. The complex and dynamic channel environments can degrade communication performance as well as covert transmission. Therefore, this paper proposes an intelligent evaluation algorithm for covert transmission and performance based on federated learning (FL) and a Gramba Neural Network. First, a covert communication model assisted by intelligent reconfigurable surface (IRS) and artificial noise (AN) is established considering N-Nakagami fading channels. IRS is employed to reshape the propagation environment, and AN is used to disrupt signal detection. This model employs hierarchical FL with client-edge-cloud layers to protect data privacy. Edge computing is employed to reduce cloud communication overhead while adapting to data heterogeneity. This also improves privacy protection and mitigates overfitting. The Gramba neural network employs SpatSAGE, which is a spatial domain multi-hop weighted graph convolutional network with hop-interaction, for local feature extraction. A graph-aware MambaMixer is used to improve modeling of long-range dependencies. It integrates a structure-aware attention mechanism to better capture complex topological structures. Two datasets based on covert throughput (CT) and detection error probability (DEP) are generated for performance evaluation. Simulation results are presented that demonstrate superior evaluation performance compared to the GraphSAGE, GraphMamba, GAT, Graphormer and Gramba models. FL-Gramba achieves mean squared error reductions of 17.3% and 16.9% over GraphMamba with the two datasets.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3748036: With the rapid development of vehicular network technology, vehicles can obtain entertainment/safety information services through V2V and V2I communication. Vehicular intrusion detection systems (VIDSs) are essential for protecting vehicles against cyberattacks. Existing deep neural networkbased VIDSs have achieved better results in detecting malicious attack traffic. However, most systems rarely account for performance differences among vehicles, such as their computational and storage resources. In particular, the performance difference between older and the latest smart vehicles is more obvious. To accommodate vehicles with different performance levels, a twostage VIDS training framework based on federated knowledge distillation is proposed, which simultaneously produces two types of detection models: 1) a complex model and 2) a lightweight model. In the first stage, considering the distributed characteristics of the Internet of Vehicles, we designed a federated learning algorithm based on representative clients and learning quality to train complex models. This algorithm enhances the detection capability of complex models by selecting optimal model parameters. In the second stage, we design a progressive knowledge distillation algorithm that adaptively adjusts the distillation temperature to transfer detection knowledge from the complex model to lightweight models with lower resource requirements. Experiments on public datasets show that the proposed federated learning method improves the complex model's class-average accuracy, while progressive distillation enhances the detection performance of lightweight models.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3747836: Federated Deep Reinforcement Learning (FDRL) has been regarded as an emerging paradigm to empower various distributed Machine/Deep Learning (ML/DL) in 5G and Beyond. However, a number of approaches fail to jointly take into consideration the limitations of communication resource and energy capacity of Client Devices (CDs) to perform tasks, thereby hindering convergence and degrading overall model accuracy. Therefore, in this paper, we propose SAFL, a novel Simultaneous Wireless Information and Power Transfer (SWIPT)- Aided FDRL strategy with layer-wise aggregation, to realize energy/communication-efficient FL. To this end, the FL Server (FLS) adopts SWIPT to broadcast the global model to all CDs and simultaneously charges a number of resource-limited CDs for their local training. In order to balance energy/communication resource consumption and FL performance, an improved Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based Actor-Critic with Proximal Policy Optimization (AC-PPO) approach is designed to enable lightweight model uploading, by introducing entropy regularization to achieve the trade-off between action exploration and policy exploitation in DRL for layer-wise model aggregation at the FLS. Furthermore, a double-weight aggregation mechanism is designed to update the global model in an energy/communicationefficient manner. Extensive simulation experiments demonstrate that SAFL achieves optimized energy consumption and lower communication overhead without sacrificing model accuracy compared with the state-of-the-art schemes.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3748371: Deploying hierarchical federated learning (HFL) in cloud-edge-end collaborative networks has become a mainstream approach for training models without exposing raw data. However, the non-independent and identically distributed (Non-IID) nature among mobile clients (MCs), compounded by their mobility, remains a structural challenge that HFL cannot circumvent, potentially preventing the global model from reaching target accuracy or substantially increasing the latency to do so. Existing solutions primarily address these challenges from the MC perspective, through implicit data or model fusion, leaving the potential of edge server (ES) collaboration largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose an HFL under mobility via model migration (HFL-M3) framework to reduce latency.
